title: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: The more ancient a form, the more it differs from living forms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: As a general rule, the older a fossil form is, the more it differs from living forms.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: The more ancient any form is, the more, as a general rule, it differs from living forms.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On the affinities of extinct species to each other and to living species”. Scope: fossil species and genera compared with living relatives

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-13: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The relationship is measurable for many well-sampled clades, but no harmonized dataset spans the stated scope. Phylogenetic structure also makes a simple age-distance trend only moderately discriminating.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Within clades having morphological matrices, calculate distance from each fossil to extant relatives and regress it on fossil age while controlling for phylogeny and missing characters. A generally positive age-distance relation supports the claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Morphological matrices are curated for selected clades rather than all life.

Distance depends on character selection and extant survivor bias.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.79
analysis feasibility: 0.63
discriminating power: 0.54
data existence: 0.83
data adequacy: 0.58

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Age versus membership in extant genera and families is directly tabulated and is the comparison Darwin's taxonomic language supports. A regression of distance on age can be run on occurrence data in weeks, with morphospace as a check in covered clades. Living fossils and rank conventions reduce sharpness without making the age trend untestable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For fossil genera binned by age, measure taxonomic or morphological distance to the nearest living relatives and test whether that distance increases with age. No age trend, or ancient forms as similar to living ones as younger fossils are, would refute the general rule.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Character matrices cover a subset of clades.

Living-fossil exceptions are expected under a general rule and have to be scored as exceptions, which softens the test.

Taxonomic rank is a coarse stand-in for amount of difference.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.8
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.75
